title: Running LLMs locally: Practical LLM Performance on DGX Spark — Mozhgan Kabiri chimeh, NVIDIA

primary.label: Inference & Model Systems
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is serving LLMs with vLLM, measuring inference throughput and time-to-first-token, and evaluating NVFP4 quantization for inference performance. The DGX Spark is a developer workstation platform for local AI development and prototyping. The talk covers serving models in production-like Docker environments and benchmarking inference metrics. Requires familiarity with LLM serving, vLLM, Docker, and GPU memory architecture but is a practical presentation rather than deep research. This is a conference-style talk by an NVIDIA developer relations manager. All key claims are directly stated in the transcript with quantitative backing.

summary: Mozhgan Kabiri, developer relations manager at NVIDIA, presents a practical, data-backed analysis of running LLMs locally on the DGX Spark (transcript refers to it as "Jetson Spark"), powered by the GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip with 128GB unified memory and NVFP4 quantization support. She frames the motivation: as AI workloads move from experiment to production, developers face memory limitations, software stack incompatibilities, shared-infrastructure scheduling delays, and concerns around cost predictability, data residency, and deterministic latency. The DGX Spark is positioned not as a cloud replacement but as a local development platform running the same NVIDIA AI software stack as data centers, enabling desktop-to-cloud workflow continuity. Her methodology is reproducible: vLLM serving inside an NVIDIA-optimized Docker container, with an automated benchmarking harness that performs environment isolation, three mandatory warm-up runs, background GPU metrics logging at one-second intervals, and generates timestamped versioned artifacts containing metadata and benchmark results. She measures completion tokens per second and time-to-first-token via explicit streaming-response timestamping. Results show the 1.5B instruct model delivers 61.73 tokens/sec, while the 14B NVFP4 model achieves 20.19 tokens/sec—nearly 10x larger yet still faster than average human reading speed. The unoptimized 14B base model drops to 8.40 tokens/sec, proving quantization format is as important as hardware. The 14B NVFP4 model is 3.4x faster to first token than the base model. She emphasizes that memory capacity (128GB fitting up to 200B parameters) is not the same as memory bandwidth, which governs throughput; NVFP4 increases intelligence per byte. Recommended use cases: steady-state workloads, privacy-sensitive data, and rapid prototyping. Resources are available at build.nvidia.com/spark.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation for Local LLM Inference
sections.summary: Speaker introduces herself as NVIDIA developer relations manager and frames the problem: AI evolution strains developer systems with memory limits and software stack gaps, pushing workloads to cloud. As models move to production, cost predictability, data residency, and deterministic latency matter. Shared infrastructure causes scheduling delays. The question: can development workflows move closer to developers?

sections.title: DGX Spark Platform Overview
sections.summary: Introduces the DGX Spark (called 'Jetson Spark' in transcript) powered by GB10 Grace Blackwell superchip with 128GB unified memory and NVFP4 support, supporting models up to ~200B parameters locally. It runs the same NVIDIA AI software stack as production data centers, enabling minimal-change workflow migration. Positioned not as cloud replacement but as bringing AI development closer to the developer.

sections.title: Reproducible Benchmarking Methodology
sections.summary: Describes the experimental setup: vLLM serving quantized models across sizes and precision formats inside an NVIDIA-optimized Docker container matching data-center environments. An automated benchmarking harness enforces strict protocol: environment isolation, three warm-up runs, 1-second GPU metrics logging. The orchestrator generates timestamped directories with sanitized model IDs, capturing full endpoint responses and metrics as versioned artifacts.

sections.title: Time-to-First-Token Measurement Logic
sections.summary: Explains that time-to-first-token defines user-perceived performance. The script explicitly handles streaming responses from vLLM, timestamping the first chunk in the stream_once function rather than simply waiting for a complete API response.

sections.title: Throughput Results: Tokens per Second
sections.summary: Presents bar chart of completion tokens per second. 1.5B instruct model: 61.73 tokens/sec. 14B NVFP4 model: 20.19 tokens/sec despite being ~10x larger. 14B base model drops to 8.40 tokens/sec. NVFP4 quantization is identified as the hero, maintaining high intelligence at throughput faster than human reading speed. Quantization format is as important as hardware on Blackwell architecture.

sections.title: Time-to-First-Token Results and Memory Bandwidth Insight
sections.summary: Time-to-first-token results show expected increase for larger models. The 14B NVFP4 model is 3.4x faster to first token than the 14B base model. Key insight: memory capacity (128GB fitting up to 200B parameters) is not the same as memory bandwidth, which governs throughput. NVFP4 increases intelligence per byte, making a 14B model feel as responsive as a much smaller one.

sections.title: Recommendations and Resources
sections.summary: Recommends DGX Spark for steady-state workloads, privacy-sensitive data, and rapid prototyping. It enables local building and fine-tuning with the same software stack as production. Resources and playbooks available at build.nvidia.com/spark. Workflow: run locally, iterate quickly, scale to data center or cloud when ready.
